title: Canary releases
description: Gradually shift traffic to a new release and automatically roll back if health checks detect problems.

data.text: A canary release is named after the old mining practice of bringing a canary into a coal mine. If the air was toxic, the canary died before the miners did. In software, a small subset of real users or traffic tests the new version before everyone else sees it. If the canary fails, the system rolls back automatically and the majority of users are unaffected.

Canary releases require observability. You must measure latency, error rates, and business metrics in real time, compare them to a baseline, and make automatic or manual promotion decisions. Without good monitoring, a canary is just a partial rollout with no safety net.

data.title: Typical canary stages
items: 1% of traffic to the new version for 5 minutes.
Increase to 5% and watch for error-rate spikes.
Promote to 25% if health metrics remain stable.
Promote to 100% or hold for further observation.

data.text: Automated canary with Azure Deployment Manager

Azure Deployment Manager and similar orchestration tools can automate canary steps. The following conceptual YAML shows a rollout strategy that increases traffic in phases and aborts if a health check fails.

data.title: Conceptual rollout strategy
data.content: Each step promotes a percentage of traffic only if the previous step is healthy.
data.code:
rollout:
  steps:
    - name: canary-1pct
      weight: 1
      duration: 5m
      healthPolicy:
        healthyErrorRate: 0.01
        unhealthyErrorRate: 0.05
      trafficPolicy:
        endpoints:
          - target: app-green/1
            weight: 1
          - target: app-blue/1
            weight: 99

    - name: canary-5pct
      weight: 5
      duration: 10m
      healthPolicy:
        healthyErrorRate: 0.01
        unhealthyErrorRate: 0.05
      trafficPolicy:
        endpoints:
          - target: app-green/1
            weight: 5
          - target: app-blue/1
            weight: 95

    - name: promote-full
      weight: 100
      duration: 15m
      trafficPolicy:
        endpoints:
          - target: app-green/1
            weight: 100

data.text: Not all metrics are equal during a canary. Latency averages can hide tail-latency regressions that affect only a small percentage of users. Error rates are important, but business metrics such as checkout completion, login success, or search result relevance often detect problems earlier than infrastructure metrics.

terms.definition: The traffic still running the old version. Serves as the baseline for comparison.
The traffic running the new version. Also called the canary cohort.
Confidence that observed differences are real and not random noise. Critical when sample sizes are small.

data.title: Automate rollback, do not rely on humans
data.text: If a metric crosses a threshold, the system should roll back without waiting for a human to notice. Humans are slower than automated health checks and are often asleep when night-time canaries fail.

items.text: Health checks cover latency, error rate, and at least one business metric.
items.hint: Example: HTTP 5xx rate, p99 latency, checkout success.

items.text: Traffic splitting is handled by the platform, not by application code.
items.hint: Use load balancer weights, service mesh routing, or feature flags.

items.text: Rollback triggers are automated and tested in staging.
items.hint: Simulate failures to verify the system reacts correctly.

items.text: Each canary step has a defined duration and maximum traffic percentage.
items.hint: Avoid unbounded canaries that never fully promote.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Canary releases shift traffic gradually and roll back automatically on failure.
Measure infrastructure and business metrics, not just one or the other.
Automation is essential; human reaction time is too slow for canary safety.
Use canaries for high-traffic services where a bad release would affect many users.
data.takeaway: Canary releases turn risky big-bang deployments into controlled, observable experiments.

items.question: Can I run canaries without a service mesh?
items.answer: Yes. Load balancers, deployment slots, and even feature flags can split traffic. A service mesh makes it easier but is not a strict requirement.

items.question: How long should a canary step last?
items.answer: Start with 5 to 10 minutes for infrastructure metrics and 15 to 30 minutes for business metrics. The right duration depends on your traffic patterns and alert sensitivity.
